title: Dignity at work: equality and preventing harassment
siteNotes: Who staff report harassment or discrimination to (name and role), and who they go to if the complaint is about that person.
Where the written equality, dignity at work and anti-harassment policies and the grievance procedure are kept and how staff get a copy.
How guest or supplier harassment is logged and how a manager follows it up (for example an incident form), and what the venue does about a guest who harasses staff.
Any external confidential support the venue offers (employee assistance line, for example), if there is one.
GM to confirm the policy and training records satisfy the 'all reasonable steps' duty, and to re-check the date for guest and supplier harassment liability.
legalNotes: Protected characteristics (nine): age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation. Equality Act 2010 s.4. Source: https://www.gov.uk/discrimination-your-rights

Direct discrimination (s.13) is treating someone worse because of a protected characteristic; indirect discrimination (s.19) is a rule or way of working that applies to everyone but puts people with a characteristic at a disadvantage and cannot be justified. Source: https://www.equalityhumanrights.com

Harassment (s.26): unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic, or of a sexual nature, that has the purpose or effect of violating dignity or creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment. It does not have to be intended; the effect on the person counts, judged reasonably. Source: Equality Act 2010 s.26, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15/section/26
Victimisation (s.27): being treated badly because you made or supported a complaint, or are believed to have. Source: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15/section/27

Employer duty to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of employees: s.40A, inserted by the Worker Protection (Amendment of Equality Act 2010) Act 2023, in force 26 October 2024 (date as given in the index). Wording in the Act is 'reasonable steps'. Source: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/51 and EHRC technical guidance on sexual harassment at work. Could not open the EHRC page (access blocked), so not independently re-read.

Employers' liability for harassment of staff by third parties (guests, customers, suppliers): reintroduced by the Employment Rights Act 2025, reported by Acas and law firms as starting 30 October 2026, where the employer has not taken 'all reasonable steps'. Also reported: the Employment Rights Act 2025 raises the s.40A standard from 'reasonable steps' to 'all reasonable steps'. FLAG: verified only from secondary sources (Acas page https://www.acas.org.uk/employment-rights-act-2025/harassment-law-changes, law firm summaries) and I could not open the Act itself. The slides say 'from 30 October 2026' for guests; GM to confirm before use. The slides avoid the 'all' / 'reasonable' wording difference by saying 'reasonable steps'.

Raising a concern and Acas guidance on dealing with harassment and the grievance process: https://www.acas.org.uk/discrimination-and-the-law. Time limits for tribunal claims are deliberately not taught here.
The 'never just banter' point is guidance: under s.26 the intention of the person does not decide whether it is harassment.

Review Oct 2026: 30 October 2026 for (a) employer liability for third-party harassment of staff on any protected characteristic and (b) raising s.40A from 'reasonable steps' to 'all reasonable steps' confirmed by Acas (https://www.acas.org.uk/employment-rights-act-2025/harassment-law-changes) and several law firms. The commencement regulations themselves were not read, so GM/Ward Hadaway should confirm they are made. Government has said the standard for third-party harassment will be lower than for harassment by the employer's own workforce, and regulations defining 'all reasonable steps' are not expected until 2027 or later.

Review Oct 2026: slide 5 previously implied the guest duty only began on 30 October 2026. Sexual harassment by third parties already falls within the s.40A duty (since 26 October 2024), so the slide now says so; the new element is liability for third-party harassment related to other protected characteristics and the 'all reasonable steps' test. Marriage and civil partnership is protected in employment only, not in the provision of services, so 'guests in most cases' replaces 'guests alike' on slides 1 and 8.

cards.title: Dignity at work: equality and preventing harassment
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- name the protected characteristics and spot unfair treatment
- recognise harassment, including from guests and suppliers
- raise a concern, and know you are protected for doing so

cards.title: Nine protected characteristics
cards.body:
The law protects us from unfair treatment because of these nine things: colleagues at work, and guests too in most cases.

This covers recruitment, shifts, pay, training, promotion and how people are spoken to day to day.

items: Age
Disability
Gender reassignment
Marriage and civil partnership
Pregnancy and maternity
Race
Religion or belief
Sex
Sexual orientation

cards.title: Direct and indirect
cards.body: Discrimination is not always loud or deliberate. It can be a plain decision, or a rule that looks fair but quietly shuts some people out.

left.title: Direct
items: Not offering a young mum extra shifts because she has children
Refusing a table because of a guest's race
Passing over a worker because of their age

right.title: Indirect
items: A rule for everyone that disadvantages one group and cannot be justified
A uniform rule that ignores religious dress
Training only held at times some people cannot attend

cards.title: What counts as harassment
cards.body:
Harassment is **unwanted behaviour** linked to a protected characteristic, or of a sexual nature, that violates someone's dignity or creates an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive atmosphere.

> It does not matter if it was meant as a joke. What counts is the effect on the person, and whether that reaction is reasonable.

items.title: Words
items.text: Jokes, nicknames, comments on bodies or background

items.title: Messages
items.text: Texts, images, social media, group chats

items.title: Actions
items.text: Touching, blocking the way, staring, gestures

cards.title: It is never just banter
cards.body:
Kitchens, bars and staff rooms can be full of teasing. Some of it is friendly. Some of it is not, and the person on the end often laughs along because they feel they must.

If someone looks uncomfortable, stop. If you are the one on the end, you are allowed to say it is not okay.

left.title: Fine
items: Teasing everyone takes well and can stop at any time
Laughing with people

right.title: Not fine
items: Jokes about race, sex, age, religion, sexuality or disability
Comments on bodies or sex lives
Carrying on after someone says stop

cards.title: When it comes from a guest
cards.body:
Harassment from a guest, a wedding party member or a supplier is still harassment. Nobody on our team has to put up with it as part of the job.

Employers already have to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of staff, including by guests. From 30 October 2026 employers are also legally responsible for harassment of staff by guests and suppliers linked to any protected characteristic, unless they took all reasonable steps to prevent it. Your part is to tell your manager each time.

items.title: Step away
items.text: If you can, leave the situation calmly.

items.title: Report it
items.text: Tell your manager the same day.

cards.title: Preventing sexual harassment
cards.body:
Since 26 October 2024 an employer must take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of its staff. From 30 October 2026 the standard rises to all reasonable steps. That is not just a policy in a drawer.

It means training like this, clear ways to report, and managers who act. Your manager will show you the policy and who to talk to.

items.title: Know the rules
items.text: Read the policy and take this training

items.title: Speak up
items.text: Report what you see or experience

items.title: Managers act
items.text: Concerns are taken seriously and followed up

cards.title: How to raise it, and why you are protected
cards.body:
You can raise a concern about something that happened to you or that you saw. Start with your manager, or another manager if it is about them. Your manager will show you who to go to.

**Victimisation** is treating someone badly because they complained or backed a complaint. It is unlawful, even if the complaint is not upheld.

items.title: Say so if you feel safe to
items.text: Tell the person it is unwelcome.

items.title: Tell your manager
items.text: Verbally or in writing, with dates if you can.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Nine characteristics are protected: for colleagues, and for guests in most cases.
- Harassment is judged by its effect, not by whether it was meant as a joke.
- Guest and supplier harassment is not part of the job: report it every time.
- Never punish or freeze out someone who raises a concern.

cards.q: Lena tells a chef his jokes about her accent make her uncomfortable. He says it is only banter and he meant no harm. Which is true?
options: It cannot be harassment because he did not mean it that way
It can still be harassment because the effect on her is what counts
It only counts if she complains in writing
It only counts if other people heard it
cards.why: Harassment is judged by the effect of the behaviour on the person, not by the intention. Writing or witnesses are not required to raise it.

cards.q: A guest at a wedding repeatedly makes sexual comments to a waitress. Because he is a guest and not a colleague, it is not something she needs to report.
cards.why: Harassment from guests still matters. She should tell her manager, who has a duty to take reasonable steps to prevent it.

cards.q: A rule says everyone must work every Sunday morning, with no exceptions. A staff member who attends a religious service then loses shifts. What might this be?
options: Direct discrimination, because the rule names a religion
Nothing, because the rule applies to everyone equally
Possibly indirect discrimination, as the rule disadvantages a group
Victimisation, because the person raised a complaint about the rule
cards.why: A rule that applies to everyone can still be indirect discrimination if it puts a protected group at a disadvantage and cannot be justified.

cards.q: Which TWO of these are protected characteristics?
options: Having a second job
Religion or belief
Being a smoker
Pregnancy and maternity
Supporting a football team
cards.why: Religion or belief and pregnancy and maternity are two of the nine. The others are not protected characteristics.

cards.q: Sam reported a colleague's inappropriate messages. Now the colleague's friends on the rota stop speaking to Sam and Sam keeps getting the worst shifts. What is this?
options: Victimisation, which is unlawful
Normal team politics
Fine, as long as no one shouts
Only a problem if the complaint is proved
cards.why: Treating someone badly because they raised a concern is victimisation. Sam should tell a manager again. It applies even if the original complaint is not upheld.

cards.q: A manager keeps giving the best shifts to younger staff and says older colleagues 'won't keep up'. What is this?
options: Fair, because he is the manager
Direct discrimination because of age
Victimisation
Only indirect discrimination
cards.why: Treating people worse because of a protected characteristic, here age, is direct discrimination.

cards.q: Since 26 October 2024, an employer must take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of its staff. Having a policy in a drawer is enough to meet this.
cards.why: The duty is about acting: training, clear ways to report, and managers who follow concerns up.

cards.q: A kitchen team teases a new starter about her weight and she laughs along, though she looks upset. What should you do?
options: Join in, since she is laughing
Stop, and tell a manager if it continues
Nothing, it is only banter
Wait for her to complain in writing
cards.why: Laughing along does not mean it is welcome. Stop, check she is alright, and raise it if it carries on. It is never just banter when it upsets someone.

cards.q: A guest has grabbed a barmaid's arm and made a lewd remark. After stepping away, what is the best next step?
options: Tell your manager the same day and note what happened
Keep quiet for now, as making a scene could upset other guests
Post about it in the staff group chat so colleagues can watch out
Wait a month to see whether he does it again before saying anything
cards.why: Tell your manager the same day and note who, what, when and where, so the venue can take reasonable steps.

cards.q: You are unhappy about something your manager has said to you. Who can you raise a concern with?
options: Nobody at all, because it has to be that manager
Another manager, who your own manager will point you to
Only a guest, as they see how the team behaves
Only the police, as it is a legal matter
cards.why: If the concern is about your manager you can go to another manager. Your manager will show you who.
